<PubmedArticle><MedlineCitation Status="MEDLINE" Owner="NLM" IndexingMethod="Manual"><PMID Version="1">27058924</PMID><DateCompleted><Year>2017</Year><Month>11</Month><Day>28</Day></DateCompleted><DateRevised><Year>2017</Year><Month>12</Month><Day>01</Day></DateRevised><Article PubModel="Print-Electronic"><Journal><ISSN IssnType="Electronic">1872-7549</ISSN><JournalIssue CitedMedium="Internet"><Volume>307</Volume><PubDate><Year>2016</Year><Month>Jul</Month><Day>01</Day></PubDate></JournalIssue><Title>Behavioural brain research</Title><ISOAbbreviation>Behav Brain Res</ISOAbbreviation></Journal><ArticleTitle>A&#x3b2;1-42-induced dysfunction in synchronized gamma oscillation during working memory.</ArticleTitle><Pagination><StartPage>112</StartPage><EndPage>119</EndPage><MedlinePgn>112-9</MedlinePgn></Pagination><ELocationID EIdType="doi" ValidYN="Y">10.1016/j.bbr.2016.04.003</ELocationID><ELocationID EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">S0166-4328(16)30195-4</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText>Amyloid-&#x3b2; peptide (A&#x3b2;) is recognized as a causative factor for the cognitive impairments in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The studies on the effects of A&#x3b2; to cognitive impairments are beneficial for lifting the veil of the pathophysiology in AD. Neuronal oscillations are proposed to play an important role in cognition and its ensuing behavior. Specially, the synchronized gamma oscillations are essential for the successful execution of working memory. However, whether the A&#x3b2; will induce the abnormal neuronal oscillations and working memory deficits has remained largely unexplored. In the present study, rats (control and A&#x3b2;-injected groups) were trained to perform a delay-alternation task on Y-maze while spikes and local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded from multi-electrodes implanted in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), an area that is strongly modulated by working memory. Synchronized neuronal oscillations were assessed by phase locking between spike trains and LFPs. We found the significant working memory impairment in the A&#x3b2;-injected group. Moreover, in the control group, during the memory retention period, a transient burst of gamma synchronization preceded an animal's correct choice, but not an animal's error choice. In the A&#x3b2;-injected group, however, gamma synchronization experience no change in neither correct nor error trials. Our results indicate that the A&#x3b2;1-42-induced dysfunction in gamma synchronization may provide a potential mechanism for working memory deficits.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright &#xa9; 2016.
